extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general educated readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Locke's distinctions and criteria about simple ideas of sensation, the taxonomy of qualities in bodies (primary/secondary/other), and the nature of perception and its relation to judgment and habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of IDEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatsoever the mind perceives IN ITSELF, or is the immediate object of perception, thought, or understanding, that I call IDEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes an idea as what is present in the mind. Locke contrasts this with qualities of external objects which are powers to produce ideas; examples and repeated usage throughout the chapter clarify that 'idea' refers to internal perceptions (e.g., ideas of white, black, pain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of QUALITY (power to produce ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to produce any idea in our mind, I call QUALITY of the subject wherein that power is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a snowball's power to produce ideas of white, cold, round is its quality. Locke uses this to separate what exists 'in the mind' (ideas) from what in objects merely has the power to produce those ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary (original) qualities of bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary qualities: SOLIDITY, EXTENSION, MOTION or REST, NUMBER or FIGURE — wholly inseparable from body and really exist in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues these qualities persist under division (grain of wheat example), exist whether perceived or not, and are the real features in bodies that resemble our ideas (i.e., ideas of shape, number, motion are resemblances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities are powers to produce sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities (colours, smells, tastes, sounds etc.) are not really in bodies but are powers, resulting from the primary qualities, to produce in us certain ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains secondary qualities depend on bulk, figure, texture, and motion of insensible particles; examples include colour and smell of a violet. He emphasizes these ideas have no resemblance to anything in the bodies themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold taxonomy of qualities in bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities in bodies are of three sorts: (1) primary (bulk, figure, number, situation, motion/rest); (2) powers to produce ideas in us (sensible/secondary qualities); (3) powers to change other bodies (qualities that alter other things' bulk/figure/texture/motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke gives examples: (2) colours/smells; (3) the sun making wax white or fire making lead fluid. He notes the first are 'real' in things, the latter two are powers resulting from primary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary qualities produce resemblances; secondary do not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of primary qualities are resemblances of patterns that really exist in bodies; ideas of secondary qualities have no resemblance in the bodies themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses contrastive examples (figure vs colour) and points out that pain, sweetness, whiteness are effects of operations and not literally in the objects producing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities twofold (immediately vs mediately perceivable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities may be (a) immediately perceivable by operating on our bodies to produce ideas, or (b) mediately perceivable by operating on other bodies to change them so they produce different ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's distinction clarifies how some powers act directly on senses (colours, smells) while others act by changing other things (sun altering wax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas from privative causes can be positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas produced by privative causes (absences) may be regarded as positive ideas in the understanding (e.g., shadow produced by absence of light is a clear positive idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues a privation in an external subject can still produce a distinct idea in the mind; he uses shadow and darkness as examples and discusses debate over whether rest is a privation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative names need not correspond to positive ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Some negative terms (e.g., SILENCE, INVISIBLE) signify no positive idea but only the absence of certain ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke cautions that while some absences produce ideas, other negative names merely denote negation and do not point to any mental image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ideas in the mind from causes in things
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding considers ideas as positive and distinct without attending to the external causes that produce them — that inquiry belongs to the nature of things external to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke stresses it is one thing to perceive and know an idea (e.g., whiteness) and another to examine the physical particles and arrangement causing that appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: How bodies produce ideas — motion/impulse via organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies operate on one another by impulse (motion); insensible particles affecting our organs convey motion to nerves/animal spirits and so produce ideas in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke asserts it is impossible to conceive body operating where it does not touch, hence perception requires some transmitted motion; this underpins his account of both primary and secondary qualities producing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities explained by insensible particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of colours, smells, tastes, and sounds are produced by insensible particles of particular figure, bulk, and motions affecting the organs of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites us to suppose that variations in the motion and figure of minute particles cause the specific sensations (violet causing blue and sweet scent), and that God could annex ideas to motions without resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception defined (first idea of reflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: PERCEPTION, as the first faculty exercised about our ideas, is the first and simplest idea we have from reflection (sometimes called thinking in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes bare passive perception from active thinking with voluntary attention; perception is what one notices when one sees, hears, feels, or thinks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception requires notice — impulse on organ insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An external impulse on a sensory organ is not sufficient for perception; the motion must be continued to the brain and taken notice of by the mind to produce an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one may have sound impulses on the ear without hearing if the mind is intently occupied — perception fails when the mind does not register the impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception vs judgment — judgment can alter sensation unconsciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas received by sensation are often altered by the judgment without conscious notice; habit and experience cause the mind to reinterpret sensory appearances as their causes (e.g., seeing a convex body as round).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke offers the blind-man-turned-sighted thought experiment (cube vs sphere) to show learned associations between senses cause judgments that are mistaken for direct perception; he emphasizes sight especially is subject to this.

rubrics_metrics.name: How habit makes sensation pass as judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: By custom and rapid mental action, habitual judgments transform bare sensations into judgments so quickly they escape notice and are taken to be direct perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes the mind's facility and habits allow many complex operations to feel instantaneous; habitual associations (e.g., reading, spoken by-words) operate without conscious attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the inlet of all knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is the first step toward knowledge; the fewer senses or the duller the impressions and faculties, the more remote one is from knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues perception is the material source for all knowledge, contrasts degrees of perception across animals and degraded human faculties (old age), and treats perception as the boundary between animals and plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same external cause may yield different sensations due to organism state
rubrics_metrics.description: The same object (e.g., water) may produce different ideas (hot for one hand, cold for another) because sensations depend on the relative motion/state of the perceiver's animal spirits or nerves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that sensations of warmth or coldness correspond to increases or diminutions of internal motion; hence comparative states of the organism determine the felt quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples demonstrating secondary qualities vanish without perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours, sounds, tastes, and odours as particular ideas vanish when perception ceases and reduce to their causes (bulk, figure, motion); e.g., porphyry has no colour in the dark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples (porphyry in darkness, pounding an almond altering taste/colour) to argue that secondary qualities are not intrinsic attributes but powers contingent on interaction and perception.
